meta.one_idea: A function is a named block written once. def only stores it; a call runs it, by jumping into the block and coming back. An argument sends a value in, and return hands a value back out.
outcomes: Write a function with def, a name, brackets, a colon and an indented block.
Say why a function that is defined but never called prints nothing.
Follow a call: Python jumps to the block, runs it, then comes back to the line after the call.
Explain the NameError when a function is called before its def.
Pass a value with greet(word=name), and say why msg made inside is unknown outside.
Use return to get a value back, and say why a line after return never runs.

build_contract: One self-contained HTML file. It opens offline from a USB stick and makes no network request.
It opens in presenter view. There is no sidebar, top bar or button the instructor has to use.

Right arrow or the clicker is one press. Left arrow goes back one press. F goes full screen, A shows all the cards, and End shows the whole card at once. The instructor guide tells the instructor these keys, so they must work.
Every card is its own screen, in the order of this spec. Press 1 is what shows when the card opens.
Every card's outer element carries data-spec="<card id>" and data-presses="<number of presses>". The review script reads both.
No link to any other file. The students' handout and the instructor guide are separate files, and a link from this file is how a class finds the answers.
rules: No autoplay. Nothing moves on a timer. One press, one move, with a caption that says what just happened.
Commit, then reveal. Where a card asks a question, the answer shows only on the press after the room has answered.
Wrong answers stay private. No names, no per-student results on screen. Hands are counted out loud, never shown.
The topic is named once. Nothing before the title card says today's topic, not a heading, not a caption, not a file name on a code card.

Words are exact. Words in quotation marks, and every line under Exact words, are final. The rest of a press describes what happens, in your own design. If an exact line does not fit, ask for a new one; do not rewrite it.
Code is exact. Copy code and outputs from the JSON, never retype them. Every output here came from running the program.
Simple English. Short sentences, everyday words. No em-dashes anywhere, the page title included.
Every card moves. A card that introduces an idea steps; a static card is a picture of a lecture.

cards.title: Recap: find the line
cards.purpose: Deck slides 9 and 10, the daily challenge. Pull back session 21's split and counting from the end: list_b[n] is always the last item, list_b[n-i] steps back.
cards.heading: Which line is to blame?
show: We want the first list forwards and the second list backwards, side by side.

presses.screen: The story line <q>We want the first list forwards and the second list backwards, side by side.</q>, the program with line numbers (deck slide 9), the input <q>1,2,3</q> and <q>4,5,6</q>, and under it <q>It prints:</q> <q>1 6 / 2 6 / 3 6</q> beside <q>We wanted:</q> <q>1 6 / 2 5 / 3 4</q>. The question <q>Which line is to blame?</q>
presses.say: This was your daily challenge. Pick a line number. Line 6? Hands up. Line 7? Line 8?
presses.room: Hands up for a line number.

presses.screen: Line 7 lights up as the culprit. The why line shows: <q>list_b[n] is the last item on every pass. list_b[n-i] steps back one place each pass.</q>
presses.say: What should line 7 say? Take answers before the next press.

presses.screen: Line 7 becomes <q>num_2 = list_b[n-i]</q> and the output changes to <q>1 6 / 2 5 / 3 4</q>.
presses.say: n minus i: 2, then 1, then 0. The second list walks backwards.

code.src:
list_a = input().split(",")
list_b = input().split(",")
len_of_list_a = len(list_a)
n = len_of_list_a - 1
for i in range(len_of_list_a):
    num_1 = list_a[i]
    num_2 = list_b[n]
    result = str(num_1) + " " + str(num_2)
    print(result)

list_a = input().split(",")
list_b = input().split(",")
len_of_list_a = len(list_a)
n = len_of_list_a - 1
for i in range(len_of_list_a):
    num_1 = list_a[i]
    num_2 = list_b[n-i]
    result = str(num_1) + " " + str(num_2)
    print(result)

cards.purpose: Predict what the party TV shows for five small programs: one call, two calls, the def at the bottom, no call, only a def.

setup.object: the party TV at Teja's party, showing each printed line as it lands, beside the program with a marker on the line Python is running; on a call the marker jumps up into cheer's block and back

rounds.ask: What does the party screen show?
rounds.program:
def cheer():
    print("Hurray!")

print("Cake")
cheer()
print("Candles")
rounds.because: Line 1 only stores cheer. Line 5 calls it, so Hurray! comes between Cake and Candles.

why.Hurray!\nCake\nCandles: That runs the block where it is written. A def only stores it.
why.Cake\nCandles: cheer() on line 5 calls it, so the block runs there.
why.Hurray!\nCake\nHurray!\nCandles: The def does not print. Only the call does.

code.src:
def icing_cost(text):
    letters = 0
    for ch in text:
        if ch != " ":
            letters = letters + 1
    return letters * 5

cake_1 = input()
cost_1 = icing_cost(text=cake_1)
print(cost_1)
cake_2 = input()
cost_2 = icing_cost(text=cake_2)
print(cost_2)
